items.rationale: The difference is who owns the control flow: in a workflow the code fixes the steps and their order in advance, and in an agent the model chooses its next step as it goes. Both can use models and tools (a), and both can run several calls (b) or handle many questions (d).

In a workflow the order of steps is written into the code ahead of time. A model may produce text or a label inside a step, but it does not choose what runs next. Answering 'the model' describes an agent.

The steps are the same every time, so a fixed workflow does the job with fewer model calls, lower cost and more predictable behavior. Calling tools does not make something an agent (a); a workflow can call tools and pass results between steps (b, c).

The model only produces a label; the code decides what runs next by branching on it, and the set of pipelines is fixed in advance. This is a routing workflow. The model is not choosing among open-ended next steps (b), the student's message is only input (c), and a variable label does not remove the code's control (d).

The agent makes 6 x 100 = 600 calls and the workflow makes 2 x 100 = 200 calls, a difference of 400. Per question the difference is 4 calls. This is why a fixed workflow suits a budget when the steps are predictable.

Finding a slot across machines and the student's training status has no fixed sequence: how many machines to check and what to do when a slot is taken depends on what comes back, so the model must choose steps as it goes. The other requests have a known, short sequence of steps that a fixed workflow handles.
